items.title: Black Friday deals bring Thunderbolt 5 docks for Mac down to $232.74
items.content_html:
Make your Mac even more useful by adding more ports, thanks to these Black Friday deals on Thunderbolt docks.

Apple's desktop Macs generally have more ports than its MacBooks. Add a display, external storage, and a few accessories, and those ports can fill up quickly.

A Thunderbolt dock lets you connect displays, external drives, and wired Ethernet through a single port on your Mac. Several docks also deliver up to 140W to a compatible MacBook Pro over that same cable.

Our picks include models with built-in SSD slots, 10Gb Ethernet, and support for multiple high-resolution displays. How many displays you can connect depends on your Mac model.

Get Thunderbolt dock deals

CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock

The CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock adds 15 ports, including three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports rated at 80Gbps each. Its host port delivers up to 140W to a compatible MacBook Pro.

The dock has three USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, and three audio connections. It also includes 2.5Gb Ethernet and UHS-II readers for SD and microSD cards.

CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock

DisplayPort 2.1 and the downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports handle video output. The dock supports up to two 6K displays at 60Hz, or two 8K displays at 60Hz on compatible Macs.

Get CalDigit TS5 deal

The CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock starts at $349.95 for Black Friday. It includes a 240W power supply.

CalDigit TS5 Plus

The CalDigit TS5 Plus has 20 ports, including two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports and 10Gb Ethernet. Its host port delivers up to 140W to a compatible MacBook Pro.

CalDigit TS5 Plus

Five USB-A ports and five USB-C ports support speeds up to 10Gbps. Separate USB controllers let the front and rear ports use their own bandwidth.

The dock includes DisplayPort 2.1 and supports up to two 8K displays at 60Hz on compatible Macs. Macs with M5 Max can drive up to four 6K displays at 60Hz.

Get CalDigit TS5 Plus deal

The CalDigit TS5 Plus is on sale for $449 at Amazon. It includes a 330W power supply and a two-year warranty.

iVanky 26-in-1 FusionDock Ultra

The iVanky 26-in-1 FusionDock Ultra is designed for Macs and has four downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports. It also includes 10Gb Ethernet for connecting to a local server or network storage.

Compatible Macs can drive up to four 6K displays or two 8K displays at 60Hz. Available display configurations depend on the Mac model.

iVanky 26-in-1 FusionDock Ultra

The dock supplies up to 140W to a compatible MacBook, and a separate USB-C port delivers up to 45W. It also has an SD 4.0 card reader and a Toslink optical audio port.

Get iVanky FusionDock Ultra deal

The iVanky 26-in-1 FusionDock Ultra is available for $599.99 ahead of Black Friday. The dock uses a built-in fan and copper heat sinks for cooling.

Ugreen Revodok Maxidok Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station

The Ugreen Revodok Maxidok Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station has 17 ports, including two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports and 2.5Gb Ethernet. It also has three 10Gbps USB-A ports and three 10Gbps USB-C ports.

The dock supports up to two displays on compatible Macs through its Thunderbolt 5 ports and DisplayPort 1.4 output. Connecting an HDMI display through DisplayPort requires an active adapter or cable.

Ugreen Revodok Maxidok 17-in-1

A built-in M.2 slot accepts PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSDs up to 8TB. The dock also has SD and microSD card readers and three 3.5mm audio jacks.

Get Ugreen Maxidok deal

The Ugreen Maxidok Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station is $319.99. Two of its USB-C ports share up to 60W for charging accessories.

Anker Prime TB5 Docking Station

The Anker Prime TB5 Docking Station has 14 connections, including two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports and 2.5Gb Ethernet. It also has three USB-A ports, SD and microSD card readers, and an audio jack.

Anker Prime TB5 Dock review

The dock supports a single display at up to 8K at 60Hz. Video output is available through Thunderbolt 5, HDMI 2.1, or DisplayPort 2.1.

The upstream Thunderbolt 5 port delivers up to 140W to a compatible MacBook Pro. Two front USB-C ports share up to 45W for charging accessories.

Get Anker Prime TB5 deal

The Anker Prime TB5 Docking Station is currently priced at $309.99. It includes a Thunderbolt 5 cable and a two-year warranty.

Wavlink Intel-Certified Thunderbolt 5 Dock

The Wavlink Intel-Certified Thunderbolt 5 Dock has 12 connections, including three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports and 2.5Gb Ethernet. The host connection delivers up to 140W to a compatible MacBook Pro.

Wavlink Intel-Certified Thunderbolt 5 Dock

The dock supports up to two 6K displays on compatible Macs. Thunderbolt 5 provides 80Gbps of bidirectional bandwidth and can boost display bandwidth to 120Gbps.

Get Wavlink TB5 dock deal

The Wavlink Intel-Certified Thunderbolt 5 Dock is $232.74. A built-in M.2 slot accepts a PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD.

items.title: 'Ted Lasso' season 5 renewal has been finally been confirmed
items.content_html:
While all evidence pointed to "Ted Lasso" returning to Apple TV for multiple seasons, Apple has only just confirmed that season 5 is indeed happening.

Following claims that pre-production would begin in January 2027, Apple has confirmed that its hit show Ted Lasso has been renewed for a fifth season. Given the success of the fourth season, which drew nearly 300 million U.S. viewing minutes across two days, it's no surprise we're getting more episodes.

Back in July 2026, Jason Sudeikis, who plays the titular Ted Lasso, said he'd like to see more seasons. The following month, Apple's own Eddy Cue similarly said the series was "certainly good enough for that," and that there were "plenty of stories to go on."

The cast of Ted Lasso also reportedly signed a three-year contract in 2025, so a fifth season was effectively inevitable. No details about the plot of the upcoming season are available, and Apple hasn't announced a premiere or launch date.

As for what might happen once the show ends for good, spin-offs have always been a possibility. One featuring the character Roy Kent was heavily rumored.

items.title: Product(Red) HomePod mini & AirPods Max could be revealed soon
items.content_html:
Apple is finally expected to bring back Product(Red) through the HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max 2 with special editions of those products on or around December 1.

Apple has been releasing products under the Product(Red) banner since 2006. Special editions of various products like iPhones, cases, and accessories have been sold with a portion of the profits going to finance AIDS programs.

According to a report from Bloomberg, Apple is gearing up to release new Product(Red) hardware in honor of (Red)'s 20th anniversary. The new products will be a red HomePod mini 2 and a set of AirPods Max 2 in silver, but with a red Digital Crown.

It is certain that customers will be disappointed that the AirPods Max would only feature a red Digital Crown, but for those holding out on a new pair, it might be enough of a differentiator. A red HomePod mini 2 could be a big hit during the holiday season.

Product(Red) has appeared in many products over the years, like the iPhone 14 in 2022 and the third-generation iPhone SE that was discontinued in 2025. That iPhone SE was the last iPhone being sold with the color, though some cases and accessories still offered it.

It isn't clear why there was a gap of over two years before Apple reentered the hardware space with Product(Red) products. However, the company never gave up on the initiative fully, as it offers a dedicated website detailing the program and various things like Apple Watch faces that use the color.

December 1 is world AIDS Day and the anniversary of the organization, so Apple is expected to announce the products around that date. They would be the first Product(Red) releases since the Apple Watch Series 9 in 2023.

items.title: Jensen Huang is reinstated as Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
Despite multiple controversies and Nvidia's board announcing it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, the firm's co-founder is right back as CEO.

Following the direct intervention of President Trump, Huang is reinstated with immediate affect, after what CNBC reports were a series of discussions between him and Nvidia's board. Nvidia stock immediately climbed by over 30% as of 9:30 AM ET.

The White House has issued a statement praising the reinstatement. "President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board," it said. "We have to protect our geniuses."

Alongside this, the Nvidia board has said that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government," and that it is confident Huang "poses no national security risk."

Chair of the board, Harvey C. Jones, had been the one to address Huang's departure during Nvidia's latest earnings call. He was very firm that Huang would not be returning, but he makes no mention of that position now.

Instead, Jones has issued a statement welcoming back Huang.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," he said. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."

Interim CEO Colette Kress has reportedly clashed in the past clashed with Huang over his circular economy. This is the policy where Nvidia pays firms to buy from it, on the presumption that the expected massive profits from AI will eventually pay off.

Huang has publicly thanked Kress as she resumes her Chief Financial Officer duties, and praised Jones for his leadership as chair.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," said Huang in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

"I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process," he continued.

National security

Perhaps key to Huang being allowed to return as CEO is how Nvidia has revised its national security procedures. On November 17, 2026, five days after Huang resigned, Nvidia announced the creation of an Export Control Oversight Committee.

"As the world's leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges [of national security]," said Harvey Jones.


Trump (shown here during his first administration) told Nvidia that Huang has done nothing wrong — image credit: White House

There was no comment on what procedures Nvidia had followed before, nor any acknowledgement that the new committee followed the controversy over Huang.

Instead, Jones said that the decision "to create this new committee reflects the Board's further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Huang's resignation

The news comes after Huang said that he would return to Nvidia if the company would just ask him. The company then said it would not.

Huang resigned as CEO. The board unanimously accepted that resignation, after his multiple affairs were revealed to include one with an alleged Chinese spy.

He was replaced by Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. People including Elon Musk and President Trump, however, called for his reinstatement.

How we got here

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, and the company initially became known for producing gaming processors. However, demand for AI processors starting in late 2022 saw Nvidia's stock rise 14-fold.

The latest available figures showed that this earned Huang a personal net worth of $90 billion by May 2024. However, Nvidia's stock dropped by over $800 billion after the first revelations of Huang's affairs emerged.


Jensen Huang (left) was briefly replaced by Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress (right) as interim CEO. - images credit: Nvidia.

Ultimately he would be shown to have had three affairs, but it was the one with Alice Huang (no familial relation) that prompted the controversy. Alice Huang is alleged to have been a Chinese spy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce launched a joint investigation into the issues.

Those issues are partly that Jensen Huang may have been targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation, and therefore he may have provided confidential information. There is also a question of whether Nvidia, under Huang's leadership, has violated US export controls.

Megaspeed, a Singapore firm which had Alice Huang as an executive until August 2025, is being investigated over allegations that it provided restricted processors to China.

Alongside both of these, there is a question of how much Huang and other executives knew. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on November 19, 2026, that the DOJ was looking into whether "Nvidia misled investors and the public" about the risk of China obtaining restricted processors.

As yet there has been no word on whether Huang's reinstatement affects this DOJ investigation. At present, however, a Congressional hearing is to be held in public and live-streamed on December 3, 2026.

Chair Harvey Jones has said that Nvidia's own investigation is to continue.

items.title: EU urged to challenge Apple's grip on iPhone browsers
items.content_html:
In a new letter to regulators, businesses and advocacy groups say that even slightly loosened in the European Union, Apple's WebKit requirements still make it effectively impractical to sell subscriptions outside the App Store.

Businesses and civil society organizations are urging the European Commission to open formal proceedings against Apple over iPhone browser competition. They say Apple's restrictions still keep browser makers from moving existing EU users off WebKit.

WebKit is the browser engine Apple's Safari uses to load and display webpages. It interprets the code behind websites and determines which features they can use.

Previously, Apple required all third-party browsers to operate under this framework. The Digital Markets Act requires Apple to let rival browsers use their own engines and provide the necessary software and hardware access.

As of iOS 17.5, Apple permits alternative engines in the EU, but the groups say its technical and legal requirements make switching impractical. To this date, no single browser has made the switch.

The letter is available to read on Open Web Advocacy's site. The authors say the signatories collectively represent an estimated 45,000-55,000 EU-established businesses and organizations.

The letter argues that Apple's browser restrictions leave businesses more dependent on the App Store to reach iPhone users. Web apps would give publishers more control over subscription pricing, billing, and their relationships with readers.

The letter estimates that EU businesses could save 11 billion euros annually in development costs and 1.3 billion euros in App Store fees. That projection assumes half of native iOS app development shifts to the web.

The signatories include notable companies like Mozilla and Shopify. Open Web Advocacy says it will continue collecting signatures until December 3, 2026.

items.title: It's complicated - how to buy or sell a smart home on Smart Home Insider
items.content_html:
Between permanent wall-mounts and unpaired devices, home automation can complicate buying or selling a home. We talk about it all, on this episode of Smart Home Insider.

This episode's guest is Brandon Doyle who is a licensed realtor, a writer for Realtor Magazine, and a content creator. He has years of experience dealing with smart home devices in homes and has a few things to avoid.

Before turning to our guest, we jump into the news. Headlining this week was Apple's new beta of iOS 27.3 and tvOS 27.3.

There are two notable changes to smart home users in the Apple TV app. After this update, video podcasts will show in the Apple TV app, as will movie sequels.

A full release is expected in December. The major iOS 27.3 update also includes a new Health app, Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch users, new strength training workouts in Apple Fitness, and more.

Google officially announced the discontinuation of the Nest app. Users have until January 25, 2027 before the app stops working and until March 25, 2027 to officially migrate their account to the Google Home app.

In August, Google is also cutting off Google Assistant from its smart speakers. Users will instead have to use Google Gemini, which is more powerful and conversational.

Finally in the news, Aqara announced several new smart lights that are available to order. There is a new floor lamp, two sets of outdoor lights, updated downlights, a light strip, and two candelabra-style bulbs.

Turning to the interview, Brandon Doyle has several dos and don'ts to share. He's seen many things in his time, such as a video doorbell costing a couple $20,000 and transferred devices that aren't reset properly.

items.title: Huang 'did nothing wrong,' Donald Trump told Nvidia's board
items.content_html:
President Trump believes that his "intervention was very important" in discussions with Nvidia, ahead of the disgraced ex-CEO being reinstated.

Trump has stopped short of saying that he is responsible for the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang to the role of Nvidia CEO. But in an interview and on social media, he has called the move "the correct and proper decision," and praised how reasonable the board had been as he's talked with them "directly and indirectly."

Speaking to CNBC, Trump said that Huang "did nothing wrong."

"We've done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgement, having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents — but he did nothing wrong," said Trump. "He created a chip that's invaluable, and he's got some coming that are going to be maybe even better."

Trump has been downplaying the investigation since the start. On November 16, 2026, he said he hadn't heard that Alice Huang was a spy.

"Any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman, that comes from China, they say she's a spy," said Trump. "I don't know that she was a spy at all."

He said that seemingly before beginning to press the Nvidia board for reinstatement. In his new remarks, he has not referred to Alice Huang, and instead has concentrated on how Jensen Huang is admired all over the world.

"I just left President Xi," continued Trump in his CNBC interview following the reinstatement, "and President Xi was saying [Huang is] the most brilliant in the world at that business, and he probably is considered that by everybody. We have to protect our genius."

Asked about specifically how and why he intervened, Trump said that he had "felt more strongly" as he saw "what was happening with the company, because that was, to me a very important part of our country."

"It would've been a lot tougher [to do], if I made the call a week and a half ago," said Trump, "because everybody was riding high. They were going to run the company, it was beautiful."

"When the company crashed, they said, wait a minute, this job is no fun," continued Trump. "I think the board acted really responsibly.. some other board would've fought it [and] it would've been a disaster, in my opinion."

National security issues

Trump has now also been asked about what Jensen Huang's reinstatement means for the concerns over national security issues. "They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," he confirmed, "and [we] gave [them] assurance at least with everything we know, and we know a lot."

"I'm very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing," he said. "They suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly."

Trump was asked whether he pushed for the reinstatement because of how stocks broadly fell after the resignation. "Probably so," said Trump, "but the bigger impact was the long term."

"The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about," concluded Trump.

items.title: iPhone Duo's small outer screen may yet get more widgets
items.content_html:
Code discovered in the iOS 27 developer beta shows that Apple has tested adding two more slots for circular widgets under the status icon for the iPhone Duo.

Since iOS 16 back in 2022, it's been possible to edit the iPhone's home screen and place widgets there. The same is true on the iPhone Duo which has the same options, albeit with a slight rearrangement to fit the smaller screen.

Now as discovered by code examiner "pdfu," Apple has found a way to squeeze more widgets onto the iPhone Duo's lock screen than on the other iPhones in the range. Describing them as being in a "complication column," pdfu says that the new widgets are circular ones that can lie in a vertical line.

Apple has tested a "complication column" for iPhone Duo's Lock Screen. It fits two circular widgets along the right edge.

Flag: SpringBoard/Ionic (disabled). First seen in iOS 27.1, with no code changes since.

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 22, 2026

This positioning means that the two slots for circular widgets lie in a vertical line that has the iPhone Duo's new status icon at the top. At the bottom of this line, the iPhone Duo already has one or two customizable icons, typically including the camera.

If Apple chooses to enable these extra circular widgets, they would be placed beneath the status icon and above the Focus Mode one.

That Focus Mode widget is the reason that this new addition has to be limited to two icons. While the Focus Mode icon is only displayed when a user has turned on Do Not Disturb or similar, Apple is leaving the space clear for it.

Code sleuth pdfu says that this feature was first spotted in code for the iOS 27.1 developer beta. It remains in the latest iOS 27.3 and has had no code changes.

The fact that it still hasn't been released could mean that Apple has decided against it. However, it's more likely that the company would remove the code entirely if it were really never going to make it available for use.

It was pdfu who first discovered how Apple was rearranging the iPhone Duo's screen. They also specifically uncovered how the Focus Mode icon would be updated to be more useful.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Siri AI limits and the possibility of pettiness
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, Apple's pettiness is on full display in the UK, though it's entirely unclear why Apple decided not to extend Siri AI limit increases to the country.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Higher limits, but not for these specific countries

As an organization, Apple has disagreements with practically every major government on the planet in some form. Most of the time, it's business as usual and doesn't affect the normal services Apple provides to customers.

Most, that is, not all of the time. Sometimes, Apple makes decisions against specific entities benefiting from something that everyone else already enjoys.

A big example of that is the whole EU Digital Markets Act spat, which basically enabled Apple to stop some AI-based services from working in the bloc at all. All under the claim that there needs to be a way to preserve privacy despite the EU's regulation.

That's been a problem that has persisted for many years, and will still do for years to come. Sadly, it's a glacial experience waiting for a multinational giant and a continental government agency to blink first.

At the very least, there's some rhyme or reason for that happening at all.

Siri AI limit increases are happening for iCloud+ subscribers, except not in the UK for some reason... - Image Credit: Parliament

When it comes to Apple's decision to introduce daily Siri AI allowances, Apple wasn't so forthcoming with a reason.

On November 16, Apple said that there were allowance extensions for subscribers of iCloud+. It was available everywhere Siri AI was potentially usable, except a small list of regions.

China makes sense to be excluded, as it doesn't have Siri AI yet. So do EU countries in general, as it's a continuation of the existing spat.

However, for Brazil, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, there's no immediately apparent reason at all from Apple.

For the UK, it's especially annoying, since we have Siri AI access enabled already. All the block does is stop iCloud+ subscribers from being able to get more allowance.

It is an extraordinarily picky decision to prevent the UK from getting more of a benefit from something it already can use. Blocking access completely to something when it wasn't available before would make more sense, but this doesn't.

Maybe it's justifiable?

Sure, Apple and the UK don't see eye to eye on matters like the App Store and continual demands for backdoor access to iCloud data. Heck, Apple even turned off Advanced Data Protection in the UK in early 2025 because of a law change, and refused to reinstate it.

It doesn't help the UK that a tribunal ruled in favor of Apple on November 19, forcing the UK government to admit there was an order to try and get access to encrypted user data.

To be clear here, the problem is less about the existence of the demand for access, as that's something everyone's complained about previously in various ways. The issue is the UK deciding to use laws to try and gag Apple from discussing the matter at all.

The UK government gag order certainly prevented Apple from talking, and to its credit, it stayed quiet. It's just that the UK government didn't take into account that media in other countries would report about it.

It's one thing for Apple to be ordered to do something and to resist every step of the way. It's another to keep an order that affects the general public hidden from view.

Apple blocked ADP in the UK over encryption-breaking demands and regulation. The Siri AI thing seems trivial in comparison.

We don't know if Apple is lashing out at the UK with this Siri AI limit exclusion because of this matter. The timing is very coincidental, but it also seems like an extremely unusually minor response compared to closing access to an entire service, as it did before.

As it stands, the decision to not allow more of a Siri AI limit to people paying for iCloud+ in the UK is a very picky and petty thing to do, seemingly without that much tech-wise to get in the way.

It's the country-wide version of Apple wishing you to have an annoying, ever-present bubble under your iPhone's screen protector.

It's mildly annoying, but more confusing about why the decision was made in the first place.

Hopefully Apple will eventually give some explanation, even a half-hearted one, to nod for why this has happened.

As it stands, all we can do is make wild speculation and imagine Apple with a chip on its shoulder. One that only it knows why it exists.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed the commentator's curse with CEO antics, and whether hardware reviewers need to learn new skills like robotics.
